title: How does @Column control field-to-column mapping, and what is the difference between JPA @Transient and the Java transient keyword?
shortTitle: @Column mapping + @Transient — field-to-column control and excluding fields from persistence

s1_definition.profdef: `@Column` fine-tunes how an entity field maps to a database column: `name` sets the column name, `nullable = false` adds a NOT NULL constraint, `length` sizes a `VARCHAR`, `precision`/`scale` size a `DECIMAL`, `unique = true` adds a unique constraint, `updatable = false`/`insertable = false` exclude the column from generated UPDATE/INSERT statements, and `columnDefinition` lets you specify raw DDL. JPA `@Transient` tells the persistence provider "do NOT map this field to any column" — it is excluded from all SQL but still participates in normal Java behaviour such as serialization. The Java `transient` keyword is unrelated to JPA: it tells Java's built-in `Serializable` mechanism to skip the field during object serialization. They solve different problems: `@Transient` controls DATABASE persistence; `transient` controls JAVA serialization. A field can be one, both, or neither, and confusing the two is a common bug.
s1_definition.analogy: `@Column` is the instruction sheet telling the bank's filing clerk exactly which box each piece of customer data goes into, how long the box can be, and whether the box is allowed to be empty. JPA `@Transient` is a sticky note saying "this scratch calculation does NOT get filed in the vault at all" — like a derived total you compute on screen but never store. Java's `transient` keyword is a totally different note that only matters when you photocopy the whole file to send elsewhere (serialization), telling the photocopier to leave that field blank.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@Column` tunes name, nullability, length, precision/scale, uniqueness, and insert/update inclusion; JPA `@Transient` excludes a field from DATABASE mapping, while Java `transient` excludes it from JAVA serialization — same word idea, completely different mechanisms.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@Column` fine-tunes how an entity field maps to a database column: `name` sets the column name, `nullable = false` adds a NOT NULL constraint, `length` sizes a `VARCHAR`, `precision`/`scale` size a `DECIMAL`, `unique = true` adds a unique constraint, `updatable = false`/`insertable = false` exclude the column from generated UPDATE/INSERT statements, and `columnDefinition` lets you specify raw DDL. JPA `@Transient` tells the persistence provider "do NOT map this field to any column" — it is excluded from all SQL but still participates in normal Java behaviour such as serialization. The Java `transient` keyword is unrelated to JPA: it tells Java's built-in `Serializable` mechanism to skip the field during object serialization. They solve different problems: `@Transient` controls DATABASE persistence; `transient` controls JAVA serialization. A field can be one, both, or neither, and confusing the two is a common bug.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** `@Column` is the instruction sheet telling the bank's filing clerk exactly which box each piece of customer data goes into, how long the box can be, and whether the box is allowed to be empty. JPA `@Transient` is a sticky note saying "this scratch calculation does NOT get filed in the vault at all" — like a derived total you compute on screen but never store. Java's `transient` keyword is a totally different note that only matters when you photocopy the whole file to send elsewhere (serialization), telling the photocopier to leave that field blank.

**One line to remember:** `@Column` tunes name, nullability, length, precision/scale, uniqueness, and insert/update inclusion; JPA `@Transient` excludes a field from DATABASE mapping, while Java `transient` excludes it from JAVA serialization — same word idea, completely different mechanisms.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me walk through `@Column` first, because its options come up constantly in real schemas.

`name` maps a camelCase Java field to a snake_case column, for example `@Column(name = "holder_name")`. Without it, Hibernate applies its naming strategy, but I set it explicitly to avoid surprises. `nullable = false` generates a NOT NULL constraint in the DDL and also lets Hibernate validate early. `length` sets a `VARCHAR` size, for example `@Column(length = 10)` for a PAN. For money I never use `length`; I use `precision` and `scale` on a `BigDecimal`, for example `@Column(precision = 15, scale = 2)` meaning up to fifteen total digits with two after the decimal point — essential for correct currency storage. `unique = true` adds a unique constraint. `columnDefinition` lets me specify exact DDL like `columnDefinition = "TEXT"` when the default type is not what I want.

```java
@Column(name = "holder_name", nullable = false, length = 100)
private String holderName;

@Column(name = "balance", nullable = false, precision = 15, scale = 2)
private BigDecimal balance;         // DECIMAL(15,2) — correct for money

@Column(name = "pan", nullable = false, unique = true, length = 10)
private String pan;
```

Two subtle but powerful options are `insertable = false` and `updatable = false`. `updatable = false` means the column is set on INSERT but Hibernate never includes it in an UPDATE, which is exactly right for a `createdAt` timestamp that must never change. `insertable = false, updatable = false` together make a field read-only from the ORM's point of view, which is common when two mappings share one physical column (such as a join column that is also exposed as a plain field).

```java
@Column(name = "created_at", updatable = false)
private java.time.LocalDateTime createdAt;   // set once on INSERT, never on UPDATE
```

Now the two "transients", which trip up almost every junior. JPA's `@Transient` annotation means "this field is NOT a persistent property — never put it in any SQL." I use it for derived or computed values that I keep in memory but never store, such as a running display total or an age computed from a date of birth.

```java
@Transient
private java.math.BigDecimal displayTotal;   // computed, never a column
```

Java's `transient` keyword is from core Java and has nothing to do with databases. It affects only Java's default `Serializable` serialization: a field marked `transient` is skipped when the object is serialized to a byte stream. It does NOT affect JSON serialization by Jackson, and it does NOT affect JPA mapping.

```java
private transient String sessionCache;       // skipped by Java Serializable, but STILL a DB column unless also @Transient!
```

The dangerous confusion is assuming the Java `transient` keyword excludes a field from the database. It does not. If you want a field excluded from persistence you must use the JPA `@Transient` annotation. A field can carry both: `@Transient` to keep it out of the database and the `transient` keyword to keep it out of Java serialization, if both are desired. A senior nuance: by default JPA uses field access or property access depending on where you place `@Id`, and `@Transient` must be placed consistently with that access type; I keep annotations on fields throughout an entity to avoid mixed-access surprises.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the concrete bugs this cleared up on the account entity at National Bank of India.

Problem 1 — money was stored with the wrong precision. An early mapping stored `balance` without `precision` and `scale`, so the generated column could not reliably hold paise, and rounding errors crept into statements. This is exactly what `@Column(precision = 15, scale = 2)` fixes: it produces a `DECIMAL(15,2)` that stores rupees and paise exactly, which is non-negotiable for a bank.

Problem 2 — the creation timestamp kept getting overwritten. The `createdAt` field was included in UPDATE statements, so an account edit silently changed its "opened on" date. This is exactly what `@Column(updatable = false)` fixes: the column is written on INSERT and never touched again.

Problem 3 — a developer used the Java transient keyword expecting it to keep a computed field out of the database, and was baffled when Hibernate complained about a missing column. This is exactly the transient-versus-@Transient confusion: the Java keyword only affects Java serialization, so the field still needed the JPA `@Transient` annotation to be excluded from persistence.

Problem 4 — the PAN needed a uniqueness guarantee. Two accounts were created with the same PAN due to a race. This is exactly what `@Column(unique = true)` plus a database unique constraint enforces at the storage layer.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is an `Account` entity demonstrating the full range of `@Column` options: `name` for snake_case mapping, `nullable = false` for required fields, `length` for the PAN, `precision`/`scale` for the balance, `unique = true` for the PAN, and `updatable = false` for `createdAt`. It has a `@Transient` computed field `availableForWithdrawal` (balance minus a hold) that is calculated in a `@PostLoad` method and never stored. It also has a plain `transient` Java field to contrast the two mechanisms. The `AccountService`, annotated `@Transactional`, saves an account and reads it back, logging that the transient fields are populated in memory but absent from the SQL. A test verifies the computed field is derived correctly and is not a column.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package

# Run
java -jar target/account-column-service-1.0.0.jar

# Open an account — INSERT excludes the @Transient fields
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8365/api/v1/accounts?accountId=SAV3001&holderName=Amit%20Patel&pan=KLMNO9012P&balance=500000&holdAmount=20000"
# SQL: INSERT INTO accounts (account_id, holder_name, pan, balance, hold_amount, created_at) VALUES (...)
#      (NO availableForWithdrawal column, NO sessionCache column)

# View — availableForWithdrawal is recomputed via @PostLoad, not read from a column
curl http://localhost:8365/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001
# → {"balance":1000000.00,"holdAmount":50000.00,"availableForWithdrawal":950000.00}

# Run tests
mvn test
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is opening Amit's account with a balance of 500000 and a hold of 20000, then viewing Rajesh's account.

Step 1: `open(...)` runs in a `@Transactional` method and constructs an `Account`. The constructor sets `createdAt` to now, and we also set `sessionCache` to a scratch value.

Step 2: `accountRepo.save(account)` triggers an INSERT. Hibernate includes exactly the mapped columns: `account_id`, `holder_name`, `pan`, `balance`, `hold_amount`, and `created_at`. The `@Column(precision = 15, scale = 2)` on `balance` and `hold_amount` means they are stored as `DECIMAL(15,2)`, so rupees and paise are exact. The `@Column(unique = true)` on `pan` is backed by a unique constraint, so a duplicate PAN would be rejected at the database.

Step 3: The INSERT EXCLUDES `availableForWithdrawal` and `sessionCache` because both carry the JPA `@Transient` annotation. Crucially, the Java `transient` keyword on `sessionCache` is NOT what excludes it from the database — the `@Transient` annotation is. If the field had only the keyword, Hibernate would still try to map it to a column and fail validation.

Step 4: After the INSERT, the `@PostPersist` callback runs `computeAvailable`, setting `availableForWithdrawal` to balance minus hold, which is 500000 minus 20000 equals 480000. This value lives only in memory.

Step 5: The view flow loads Rajesh's account. Hibernate reads the stored columns, then the `@PostLoad` callback recomputes `availableForWithdrawal` as 1000000 minus 50000 equals 950000. The derived value is never read from a column because no such column exists. The `createdAt` is returned unchanged, and because it is `updatable = false`, any later edit to the account will never rewrite it.

```
2026-10-24 00:42:31 INFO  AccountService - Opened SAV3001 balance=Rs.500000.00 available=Rs.480000.00 (available is @Transient)
2026-10-24 00:42:31 FINE  AccountService - INSERT accounts(account_id, holder_name, pan, balance, hold_amount, created_at)
2026-10-24 00:42:31 FINE  AccountService - INSERT excluded availableForWithdrawal + sessionCache (@Transient)
2026-10-24 00:42:31 INFO  AccountService - Loaded SAV2001 — availableForWithdrawal computed via @PostLoad = Rs.950000.00
```

```
  │ @Entity Account                                              │
  │  @Column(name,nullable,length)        holderName : String    │ → column
  │  @Column(unique,length)               pan : String           │ → column (UNIQUE)
  │  @Column(precision=15,scale=2)        balance : BigDecimal    │ → DECIMAL(15,2)
  │  @Column(updatable=false)             createdAt : LocalDateTime│ → column (INSERT only)
  │  @Transient                           availableForWithdrawal  │ ✗ NOT a column
  │  @Transient + transient               sessionCache            │ ✗ NOT a column, ✗ not serialized
  │  @PostLoad/@PostPersist computeAvailable()                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠ Java 'transient' keyword does NOT exclude a field from the DB — use @Transient.
  ⚠ Use precision+scale (not length) for BigDecimal money columns.
  Rule: @Column for DDL control; @Transient for derived data; keyword only for Java serialization.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Column annotation lets me control exactly how an entity field maps to a database column. I set the column name to bridge camelCase fields to snake_case columns, nullable false to add a not-null constraint, length to size a varchar, precision and scale to size a decimal, and unique to add a unique constraint. For money I always use precision and scale on a BigDecimal, never length, so a balance maps to a decimal with fifteen total digits and two decimal places, which stores rupees and paise exactly. Two options I rely on for correctness are updatable false, which writes a column on insert but never on update, perfect for a created-at timestamp that must stay fixed, and the combination of insertable false and updatable false to make a field read-only when two mappings share one physical column.

The transient distinction is a classic interview trap and a real bug source. The JPA Transient annotation means the field is not persistent at all, so it is excluded from every SQL statement; I use it for derived values like available balance that I compute in memory and never store. The Java transient keyword is completely unrelated to JPA; it only tells Java's built-in serialization to skip a field when the object is turned into a byte stream, and it has no effect on database mapping or on JSON serialization by Jackson. So if I want a field kept out of the database I must use the JPA Transient annotation, and a field can carry both when I want it out of both the database and Java serialization.

In our account entity at National Bank of India, the balance and hold amount use precision and scale for exact money storage, the PAN is unique and length-limited, the created-at timestamp is not updatable so an edit never changes the opening date, and the available-for-withdrawal figure is marked JPA Transient and recomputed from the stored columns in a PostLoad callback. The senior cautions I give are to always use the annotation rather than the keyword for excluding fields from persistence, to use precision and scale rather than length for money, and to keep annotations consistently on fields to avoid mixed field-and-property access surprises.
